title: 2025-03-01-ryker-health-dedicated-capacity-usability-eval

Maya to draft benchmark plan and sample payload template for 2-week run
Customer to share QPS profile, peak window examples, and HIPAA data flow diagram
action_items: Jordan Lee: Send pricing and reserved node terms by 2025-03-04

summary: Initial discovery with Ryker Health to evaluate dedicated Redwood capacity for a latency-sensitive, HIPAA-regulated clinical assistant. Key concerns: VPC/KMS integration, guaranteed concurrency for morning triage windows, warm pool/burst strategy and fallback to hosted. They want a live benchmark run before committing.
topics: isolation & tenancy (dedicated vs shared, node fencing)
burst strategy (warm pools, pre-warm, burst windows)
benchmark plan and success criteria (p95/p99 latency, cost per 1k tokens)
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-03-01 15:00 PT | Duration: 52 minutes | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Liam (CTO), Priya (SRE Lead), Hannah (PM)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time today, I'm Jordan with Redwood Inference, this is Maya our solutions engineer. quick confirm everyone can hear me?
[00:06] Liam: Yep loud and clear.
[00:08] Priya: good here.
[00:11] Jordan: Awesome. Quick agenda — understand your current stack and constraints, isolation needs, burst profile, and then talk through our dedicated reserved GPU options and next steps. Sound okay?
[00:19] Hannah: Yep that's perfect.

[00:30] Maya: So maybe to start, can you give us a sense of the current architecture and what you're running today for inference?
[00:35] Liam: Sure, so we've got a pretty standard setup. We run EKS on AWS and have been running a mix of EC2 instances with g4dn for smaller models and trying out g5 instances for the bigger reloads. Mostly self-managed serving with Triton and some internal routing.
[00:50] Priya: And just to add — we've been seeing big variance during morning clinical triage where the throughput spikes 4x for about 45 mins. Latency p95 shoots up and it impacts the web UI.
[01:05] Jordan: Got it. So primary concerns are predictable latency for peak windows and data isolation for PHI?
[01:10] Hannah: Exactly. PHI, auditability, and also cost — we can't just keep provisioning huge fleets.
[01:16] Maya: That makes sense. On the dedicated side, we offer reserved pools that you can pin to a VPC/private deployment with KMS integration — customers often pair that with a warm pool for pre-warmed instances during peak windows.
[01:28] Priya: Quick question — is warm pool the same as pre-warm nodes or is that an ephemeral hotpool? We looked at a couple of providers and the terminology varies.
[01:35] Maya: Good callout. Our warm pool is a pre-warm layer — reserved GPU nodes kept in a lower-power warm state so they can accept work faster than cold starts; hotpool is fully provisioned but ephemeral for short spikes. We can configure both and have automatic fallback to hosted lower-latency variants if your reserved pool is saturated.
[01:49] Liam: That fallback sounds interesting — you mean falling back to Redwood hosted rather than failing requests?
[01:52] Jordan: Yeah, exactly. Policy-based routing. You can prefer dedicated for PHI where required, and non-PHI traffic or anonymized payloads can route to hosted to absorb spikes.
[02:01] Priya: How do you handle KV cache invalidation across warm nodes? We have a lot of prompt reuse and the KV cache is important for latency.
[02:08] Maya: We do continuous batching with KV cache management; cache warmups can be sticky per session. There are knobs to control cache sync frequency and eviction, and we provide telemetry for cache hit rates.

[02:30] Liam: On compliance, SOC 2 and HIPAA are hard requirements. We also have customer-managed KMS keys for encryption of cache and model artifacts. Can Redwood integrate with our KMS and produce audit logs with request-level tracing?
[02:43] Jordan: Yes — we support external KMS/HSM and produce audit logs. For HIPAA specifically, we'd work through an addendum and our private deployment can be configured so logs are forwarded to your SIEM — we also have per-request tracing.
[02:55] Priya: And SSO? We use Okta, need SAML/SCIM.
[02:59] Maya: Yep SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning supported.

[03:15] Hannah: Back to sizing: how would you recommend we size reserved nodes for the morning 45-minute window? We currently see about 600 QPS at peak with mixed short and long prompts, p95 of 1.2s right now but that's with autoscaled cluster — we'd like p95 under 500ms.
[03:30] Maya: rough rule — model choice matters most. For example, a 13B dense Llama variant will have different per-token latency than a quantized 7B. But given 600 QPS with a 45-min daily spike, many customers go with a base reserved pool sized for steady-state plus a warm pool to cover the spike. We can run a benchmark with your prompt mix to give target concurrence and exact node counts.
[03:54] Liam: We're leaning toward using a tuned 13B open model for quality. Cost-wise we can't justify 24/7 large clusters. Is burst-to-hosted an option for overflow?
[04:03] Jordan: Yes, that's what the policy-based fallback is for. Host non-PHI overflow to hosted. For PHI, we can also set soft limits and notify rather than fail — depends on policy.

[04:20] Priya: Any eviction risk with reserved? We had a provider where reserved GPUs were still preempted during cloud maintenance which killed long-running KV sessions.
[04:30] Maya: Reserved capacity is non-preemptible in our Dedicated offering — we commit capacity to you. For private/on-prem it's entirely under your control. The only time we'd shift is under extreme failure scenarios and we'd trigger failover policies.

[04:46] Hannah: What about multi-tenant isolation? We want complete hardware isolation for PHI workloads.
[04:52] Maya: We offer single-tenant nodes (physical or partitioned by card) and node fencing so your workloads never co-reside with other tenants. You can also choose VPC-private control plane.

[05:08] Liam: Let's talk numbers quickly — what's typical latency for a 13B model on an A10G-like GPU at 512 tokens with KV caching?
[05:18] Maya: ballpark — p50 ~60-120ms per token? Sorry per request depends on sequence length; for 512 tokens end-to-end we often see p95 in the 300-700ms range with warmed KV cache on modern GPUs, but we should run your exact prompts. (audio: slight overlap)
[05:36] Priya: Oo, that's a wide range. So the benchmark is required.

[05:45] Jordan: Absolutely. For pricing, reserved is monthly commit. We can put together two scenarios: 1) minimal steady-state reserved + warmpool for spikes, 2) larger reserved to avoid fallback and reduce per-token hosted costs. We'll show TCO estimates.
[05:58] Liam: Do you support quantized models that reduce GPU memory and cost?
[06:02] Maya: Yes — we support INT8/4 quant workflows and can recommend quantization that preserves accuracy. We also provide model-quality regression alerts if quant causes drift.

[06:16] Priya: For the benchmark, what should we send you? sample payloads, redaction rules, expected QPS timeline?
[06:23] Jordan: Exactly — sample prompts, average token lengths, distribution, and a list of PHI fields that must not leave the dedicated environment. The benchmark run will be scheduled on a pre-provisioned test pool.

[06:37] Hannah: About rollout — we'd want a staged pilot: 2-week bench, then 4-week pilot with a subset of traffic, then prod. Is that OK?
[06:45] Maya: That's a typical path. For pilot we can provide elevated support and runbook for failover.

[07:00] (Silence / typing)
[07:10] Liam: One concern — we have legacy data residency rules that require logs to remain in-region. Can Redwood guarantee region-local logging and metrics export?
[07:18] Jordan: Yes, region pinning for control plane telemetry and logs is supported in Private deployments and we can scope log retention to your requirements.

[07:30] Priya: Any limits on GPU types? We want to test both A10G and H100 style performance.
[07:36] Maya: We can run benchmarks on both, though H100-style clusters are more premium. We'll include both in the benchmarking plan.

[07:50] Hannah: How long does a typical reserved contract look like? annual? quarterly?
[07:55] Jordan: Most customers do 12-month reserved commits but we do 3/6/12-month flexible options with graduated discounts.

[08:05] Priya: SLA questions — what uptime guarantees and latency SLOs can Redwood commit for Dedicated?
[08:10] Maya: We have SLA-backed uptimes (99.9+ for Dedicated), and we can negotiate latency SLOs tied to your reserved capacity and model profile. We'll include service credits if SLOs aren't met.

[08:25] Liam: One more on backups — do you store model artifacts? who controls model updates?
[08:31] Maya: You can bring your own model package or use Redwood-hosted model images. For Private we can lock versions and provide an approval workflow for model rollouts. Artifacts can be stored in your customer-managed S3 with lifecycle policies.

[08:48] Jordan: Ok let's capture next steps — we'll send pricing + reserve options, Maya will send the benchmark plan, and you (Priya/Hannah) will send the traffic profile and redaction rules. Any other asks?
[08:59] Hannah: Also please send SOC2 + HIPAA attestation docs and the VPC checklist.
[09:04] Jordan: Will do.

[09:10] (Crosstalk)
[09:15] Priya: timeline-wise we want benchmark in two weeks if possible.
[09:18] Maya: two weeks is doable once we get your payloads and traffic profile.

[09:25] Jordan: Great. Thanks all — we'll follow up with the deck and the benchmark plan.
[09:30] Liam: Thanks, appreciate it.

[09:40] End of recording.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-heard technical terms (e.g., "K V cache" for KV cache), timestamps approximate, some overlapping speech. Links referenced: Redwood dedicated deck (link: redwood.com/dedicated-deck) and benchmark template (link sent post-call).
